paragraphs: This paper studies how quickly algorithms can reduce the squared gradient magnitude in smooth convex-concave minimax problems. These problems involve minimizing with respect to one set of variables while maximizing with respect to another. The quantity being tracked measures the remaining gradient signal, so the focus is on progress toward a stationary solution.

The proposed algorithms combine extragradient steps with anchoring. The authors identify this combination as an acceleration mechanism distinct from Nesterov’s acceleration. They establish an O(1/k²) rate after k iterations, improving on the O(1/k) or slower rates cited for extragradient, Popov, and gradient descent with anchoring.

The guarantee applies to the last iterate, meaning the algorithm’s current output receives the stated rate. The paper also supplies a matching lower bound, establishing optimality within the analyzed setting. Together, the upper and lower bounds show both how to achieve faster reduction of squared gradient magnitude and why that rate represents a theoretical limit for the problem framework studied.
icml-2021-accelerated-algorithms-for-smo.tldr: Combining extragradient steps with anchoring achieves an optimal O(1/k²) last-iterate rate for squared gradient magnitude in smooth convex-concave minimax optimization.

paragraphs: Adversarial purification protects an image classifier by first processing an attacked image with a separate cleaning model. The paper addresses a practical obstacle in an existing approach: purification with an energy-based model trained through Markov chain Monte Carlo can require a long sequence of updates. That makes the cleaning stage computationally demanding.

The authors instead use an energy-based model trained with denoising score matching. They show that this training approach supports purification in only a few steps. They also introduce a randomized procedure that adds noise before cleaning the image. The stated purpose is to screen the adversarial perturbation and move the image into a regime where the model can denoise effectively.

The reported evaluations show robustness against various attacks and state-of-the-art performance. The contribution therefore links the way a purification model is trained to how efficiently it can be used at prediction time. Randomization is part of the defense itself, working together with the model’s learned denoising behavior.
icml-2021-adversarial-purification-with-.tldr: A denoising-score-trained energy model purifies adversarial images in a few steps, with added random noise strengthening the reported defense.

paragraphs: An autoencoder learns to reconstruct inputs, but successful reconstruction does not necessarily mean an input belongs to the training distribution. The paper identifies missing probability normalization as a reason ordinary autoencoders can reconstruct obvious outliers well. This weakens their usefulness when reconstruction behavior is used to decide whether an example is unusual.

The proposed Normalized Autoencoder turns an autoencoder into a normalized probabilistic model. Its probability density is defined through reconstruction error, connecting the model’s ability to reproduce an input with the probability it assigns to that input. To enforce normalization, training suppresses reconstruction of negative samples. This introduces pressure against reconstructing those samples well, alongside learning the observed data.

The authors report a substantial improvement in outlier detection and experiments supporting both outlier recognition and generation of in-distribution samples. The central idea is that reconstruction becomes more informative when it is part of a normalized probability model. The same construction supports judging whether an input fits the distribution and producing samples that do.
icml-2021-autoencoding-under-normalizati.tldr: The Normalized Autoencoder uses reconstruction-based probabilities and negative samples to improve outlier detection while supporting in-distribution generation.

paragraphs: Program repair systems need examples of broken inputs paired with successful fixes. A common way to obtain them is to damage valid code using simple rules, but those artificial errors can differ from mistakes in real code. Break-It-Fix-It addresses this mismatch without requiring labeled repair pairs.

The method trains two cooperating models: a fixer that repairs code and a breaker that turns valid code into realistic broken examples. A critic, such as a compiler, checks the fixer’s attempts on real faulty inputs. Successful repairs become additional training pairs. The breaker and fixer are updated repeatedly, using their outputs and the critic’s checks to expand the paired training data.

The authors evaluate Python code with parsing errors and C code with compiler errors. They report 90.5% repair accuracy on GitHub-Python and 71.7% on DeepFix, outperforming existing methods. These findings support learning repair from real failures and automatically checked successes. Here, successful repair is tied to the specified parsing or compiler criterion.
icml-2021-break-it-fix-it-unsupervised-l.tldr: Break-It-Fix-It iteratively learns realistic code errors and critic-verified repairs, improving program repair without labeled training pairs.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Covariance Loss, a training objective that makes relationships among target variables influence what a neural network learns. Its motivation concerns predictions made from noisy observations or observations that fail to reveal some dependencies. Prior information about those relationships can help shape the mapping from inputs to targets.

The authors describe the loss as conceptually equivalent to conditional neural processes, while expressing it as a regularization term applicable to many kinds of neural networks. The learned mapping depends on target-variable relationships as well as mean activation and average dependencies between inputs and targets. This gives dependency information a direct role in the training objective.

The stated effect is greater robustness to noisy observations and the ability to recover missing dependencies using prior information. The authors investigate the loss through extensive experiments on real-world datasets with state-of-the-art models, discussing both benefits and drawbacks. The contribution is a broadly applicable training formulation for bringing that information into neural prediction.
icml-2021-conditional-temporal-neural-pr.tldr: Covariance Loss incorporates dependency information into neural-network training to improve robustness to noise and recover relationships from prior information.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning uses a learned description of how a system evolves to support decision-making. The paper points out a mismatch: these models usually describe transitions at discrete time steps, while physical systems and many control tasks evolve continuously. It proposes modeling the dynamics directly in continuous time to avoid approximating the underlying process through time discretization.

The framework combines a new actor-critic method with Bayesian neural ordinary differential equations. These equations learn the unknown rates of state evolution. Their Bayesian formulation accounts for epistemic uncertainty, meaning uncertainty about dynamics that the model has not yet established from data. The dynamics model therefore represents both an evolution rule and uncertainty about that rule.

The authors implement the approach in a new ODE-RL suite that explicitly solves continuous-time control systems. Experiments illustrate robustness to irregular and noisy data, together with sample-efficient solutions to classic control problems. The findings support continuous-time modeling as a useful foundation for learning control from imperfect observations.
icml-2021-continuous-time-model-based-re.tldr: A continuous-time actor-critic framework learns uncertain dynamics with Bayesian neural ODEs and demonstrates sample-efficient control from irregular, noisy data.

paragraphs: Learning a directed acyclic graph means estimating directed connections while ensuring they contain no directed cycles. Existing continuous optimization approaches enforce this requirement through acyclicity constraints and repeated subproblem solving. DAG-NoCurl seeks greater efficiency by developing a representation that supports searching directly within the space of acyclic graphs.

The theoretical foundation is an equivalence between weighted adjacency matrices of directed acyclic graphs and weighted gradients of graph potential functions. The algorithm uses this result in two stages. It first obtains an initial solution that may contain cycles. It then uses a graph Hodge decomposition and a projection toward the gradient of a potential function to learn an acyclic structure.

Benchmark experiments cover both linear and generalized structural equation models. The authors report accuracy comparable to baseline structure-learning methods with better efficiency, often exceeding a tenfold improvement. The contribution connects a mathematical representation of acyclicity to a practical two-step procedure, reducing the computational burden observed in those comparisons.
icml-2021-dags-with-no-curl-an-efficient.tldr: DAG-NoCurl uses graph potentials and a two-step projection procedure to learn acyclic structures with comparable accuracy and substantially better reported efficiency.

paragraphs: Graph matching methods seek correspondences between graphs, and deep-learning approaches often concentrate on learning node and edge features or improving the matching solver. This paper examines an earlier decision: how the graphs are connected in the first place. Common constructions fix connectivity using heuristics, which the authors argue may restrict model capacity and potentially reduce matching performance.

The proposed approach learns latent graph topology, or a distribution over possible topologies, to support the matching task. The authors develop two graph-generation procedures, one deterministic and one generative. The generative version emphasizes consistency across the graphs being matched, making graph construction itself responsive to the correspondence problem.

The methods outperform previous state-of-the-art approaches on public benchmarks. These results support the hypothesis that fixed heuristic connectivity can leave useful performance untapped. The contribution expands what the learning system can adapt: alongside representations and matching decisions, it can learn the underlying connection structure used to carry out matching.
icml-2021-deep-latent-graph-matching-825.tldr: Learning graph connectivity for the matching task improves reported benchmark performance over methods built around fixed heuristic graph structures.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to scale kernel ridge regression across local processors while preserving statistical accuracy. It analyzes distributed methods that use the Nyström approximation, including a version with iterative solvers. The central question is how much computation can be distributed without weakening the learning rates achieved by exact kernel ridge regression.

The authors derive optimal learning rates and improve the permitted range of processor counts relative to existing bounds. Their expectation results match exact kernel ridge regression’s learning rates while requiring essentially O(|D|^1.5) time and O(|D|) memory, where |D| denotes dataset size. They distinguish these average-over-trials guarantees from bounds in probability, which address performance in a single trial.

The paper also introduces a communication-based extension, DKRR-NY-CM, designed to improve learning performance through exchanges among processors. Both theoretical analysis and experiments support the effectiveness of this communication strategy. The work therefore addresses two connected issues: the statistical consequences of distributing approximate kernel learning and the additional value that communication can provide.
icml-2021-distributed-nystrom-kernel-lea.tldr: Distributed Nyström kernel methods attain optimal learning rates under improved processor-count bounds, with communication providing further supported gains.

paragraphs: The paper studies a strong form of neural-network expressiveness called superexpressivity. A finite collection of activation functions has this property if a fixed network architecture can approximate any multivariate continuous function to any accuracy. The architecture may depend on the number of input variables, but achieving finer accuracy requires changing only weights, without adding neurons.

Previous work had established that superexpressive activations exist, but the known functions were complicated. This paper gives simple examples and proves that the pair consisting of sine and inverse sine is superexpressive. The result shows that this unusually strong approximation capability can arise from familiar elementary functions.

The authors also show that most practical activations without periodic functions are not superexpressive. This separates the ability to approximate functions with a fixed architecture from approximation that may require increasing network size. The contribution concerns representational possibility: it establishes what suitable weights can express, with architectural size held fixed as accuracy demands increase.
icml-2021-elementary-superexpressive-act.tldr: Sine and inverse sine form a simple activation family that can approximate any multivariate continuous function using an architecture fixed by input dimension.

paragraphs: Quantum neural networks, also called variational quantum circuits, offer potential learning capabilities but present difficult training questions. This paper investigates the shape of their loss functions. It focuses on whether even simple circuits can produce optimization landscapes containing many misleading local minima, where local improvement can lead an optimizer to a suboptimal solution.

For typical under-parameterized quantum neural networks, the authors construct a dataset whose loss has a number of spurious local minima that grows exponentially with the parameter count. This is an existence result for hard datasets. They also give an almost matching upper bound, showing that the construction nearly captures the largest possible dependence considered in their analysis.

The authors attribute these quantum-network minima to quantum interference, contrasting their origin with nonlinear activations in classical networks. Experiments confirm that the constructed cases can be difficult for typical gradient-based optimizers. The work connects a quantitative landscape result to observed training difficulty on the specific hard instances it develops.
icml-2021-exponentially-many-local-minim.tldr: The paper constructs datasets that give typical under-parameterized quantum neural networks exponentially many spurious local minima and demonstrates resulting training difficulty.

paragraphs: Federated continual learning combines two demands: clients learn from private local data, and each client encounters a sequence of tasks over time. Knowledge from other clients may help with a new task, but unrelated knowledge can interfere. The paper addresses how clients can share useful information selectively within this evolving setting.

FedWeIT separates network weights into globally shared federated parameters and sparse parameters specific to individual tasks. A client receives knowledge from other clients through a weighted combination of their task-specific parameters. This gives the framework a way to control which task knowledge contributes to local learning, supporting positive transfer while reducing interference between incompatible tasks.

The authors compare FedWeIT with existing federated-learning and continual-learning methods under different levels of task similarity across clients. They report significantly better performance together with a large reduction in communication cost. These findings support distinguishing shared knowledge from task-specific knowledge and making inter-client transfer selective when tasks vary across both clients and time.
icml-2021-federated-continual-learning-w.tldr: FedWeIT selectively combines sparse task-specific knowledge across clients, improving federated continual learning while reducing reported communication costs.

paragraphs: A graph neural network can accept graphs of different sizes, but this flexibility does not by itself ensure that training on small graphs prepares it for large ones. The paper identifies a specific difficulty: local graph structures can change with graph size. Such changes occur in domains including social and biological networks.

The authors prove that differences in local structure can permit global training-loss minima that perform well on small graphs but fail on large graphs. The theorem establishes a lack of guaranteed generalization. Their empirical analysis adds that, when local structures differ, networks tend to converge to solutions that do not generalize across sizes.

Motivated by these findings, the paper suggests two approaches to improving size generalization. One is a new self-supervised task that learns meaningful representations of local structures appearing in large graphs. It improves classification accuracy on several datasets. The results make local structural coverage a concrete concern when deciding whether small training graphs adequately prepare a model for larger inputs.
icml-2021-from-local-structures-to-size-.tldr: Changes in local structure can undermine small-to-large graph generalization, and a self-supervised task targeting large-graph structures improves reported accuracy.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning learns representations from unlabeled graphs using augmented versions of the data. Its effectiveness depends heavily on which augmentations are chosen, and graph diversity makes a single manual choice difficult to reuse across datasets. The paper targets the resulting need for dataset-specific rules or repeated trial and error.

JOAO automates augmentation selection through a bi-level optimization framework instantiated as a minimax problem. The choices adapt dynamically during training. The paper also introduces augmentation-aware projection heads, routing output features through different heads according to the augmentation selected at a given training step. This makes the representation-processing stage responsive to the transformations being used.

The selected augmentations generally agree with previously observed manual best practices. Across graph datasets of different types and scales, JOAO performs comparably to, and sometimes better than, state-of-the-art competitors including GraphCL. The main practical gain is obtaining this performance without laborious dataset-specific augmentation selection, making contrastive graph learning easier to apply across varied graph data.
icml-2021-graph-contrastive-learning-aut.tldr: JOAO dynamically selects graph augmentations, matching or sometimes improving leading contrastive methods without manual dataset-specific augmentation tuning.

paragraphs: The paper connects robustness to input perturbations with generalization beyond the training distribution. It defines the out-of-distribution setting using Wasserstein distance, giving distribution shift a mathematical form. Within that formulation, the authors theoretically justify why a model that resists input perturbations can also generalize well to shifted data.

This connection motivates an analysis of adversarial training, which is used to improve perturbation robustness. The authors show convergence of excess risk on out-of-distribution data for adversarially trained models. They also study pre-training followed by fine-tuning, arguing theoretically that robustness during pre-training provides an initialization that generalizes well to downstream out-of-distribution data.

Experiments on image classification and natural language understanding support the theoretical findings. The contribution links a property of individual-input behavior to a property of performance across distributions, and extends that link to transfer through pre-training. The generalization claims are grounded in the paper’s Wasserstein-based formulation, which supplies the setting for the theoretical connection.
icml-2021-improved-ood-generalization-vi.tldr: Under a Wasserstein-based formulation, the paper connects input robustness and adversarial pre-training to improved out-of-distribution generalization.

paragraphs: Gradient regularization is a defense that does not require prior knowledge of a particular adversarial attack and adds only limited training computation. This paper asks whether changing the network’s numerical representation can make that defense more effective. It proposes a complex-valued neural network for classification problems whose inputs remain real-valued.

In the proposed network, activation derivatives depend on combinations of inputs to each layer. This allows locally stable representations to be learned around inputs used in training. The authors also identify properties of parameter derivatives that resist damage to the standard classification objective when it competes with the gradient-regularization objective. The design therefore addresses both stability and the interaction between training goals.

Experiments show better performance than gradient-regularized real-valued networks with comparable storage and computational requirements. Robust performance also approaches that of real-valued networks trained using multi-step adversarial training. These results support complex-valued network design as a way to strengthen gradient regularization while retaining its relatively limited computational overhead.
icml-2021-improving-gradient-regularizat.tldr: A complex-valued network strengthens gradient regularization, improving reported robustness over comparable real-valued networks and approaching multi-step adversarial training.

paragraphs: Intersection over union measures how much a prediction overlaps its target, but directly using the original computation for neural-network training presents gradient problems. For pixelwise prediction, absent overlap and incorrect locations can leave ineffective training signals and cause progress to plateau. Existing generalizations developed for bounding boxes do not transfer straightforwardly to this setting.

The paper proposes PixIoU, a generalized overlap measure that responds to distance when predictions and targets do not overlap, as well as to prediction location. The authors prove that it retains many properties of the original IoU. They also construct a loss and prove its submodularity, enabling the use of Lovász functions as efficient learning surrogates.

Experiments show consistent improvements over learning the original IoU across several pixelwise prediction tasks on Pascal VOC, VOT-2020, and Cityscapes. The contribution connects a more informative evaluation quantity to an optimizable training objective. Its distance and location sensitivity directly address cases where overlap alone provides inadequate guidance for improving a prediction.
icml-2021-learning-generalized-intersect.tldr: PixIoU adds distance and location sensitivity to pixelwise overlap learning, with a theoretically supported surrogate and consistent reported prediction gains.

paragraphs: Choosing a pre-trained model for a new task can be expensive if every candidate must be fine-tuned before comparison. LogME assesses candidates using their extracted features and the target labels, without fine-tuning. The paper aims to support a wider range of models and tasks than earlier assessment methods.

Its score is the logarithm of the maximum label evidence given a model’s features. The authors distinguish this evidence criterion from maximum likelihood, describing maximum evidence as immune to overfitting. They develop an algorithm that greatly reduces its computational cost. A high LogME score indicates that a candidate is likely to transfer well, providing a predictive assessment of downstream performance.

The method covers supervised and unsupervised pre-training, classification and regression, and vision and language. The authors report outperforming prior methods in their settings, with speedups of up to 3,000 times and a memory footprint of only 1% compared with brute-force fine-tuning. These findings support using inexpensive evidence-based assessment to guide model selection.
icml-2021-logme-practical-assessment-of-.tldr: LogME cheaply estimates a pre-trained model’s likely transfer performance from features and target labels without fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Weakly supervised classification uses labels produced by a corruption process, making the design of training losses especially important. The paper focuses on estimating class probabilities and asks when a loss has two desired properties: properness, which aligns the objective with probability estimation, and a lower bound, which prevents its value from decreasing without limit.

The authors first develop a representation theorem for proper losses in supervised learning that dualizes the Savage representation. They use this result to characterize proper losses for weak labels and identify a condition for lower-boundedness. This provides a theoretical basis for addressing both requirements together when designing a weak-label learning objective.

From the theory, they derive generalized logit squeezing, a regularization scheme that makes any proper weak-label loss bounded below while preserving properness. Experiments show the approach’s effectiveness compared with improper or unbounded losses. The result is both a characterization of suitable objectives and a constructive method for improving an existing proper weak-label loss.
icml-2021-lower-bounded-proper-losses-fo.tldr: Generalized logit squeezing makes proper weak-label losses lower-bounded while preserving their suitability for class-probability estimation.

paragraphs: Online patient monitoring uses evolving measurements to support the monitoring of critically ill patients. Contrastive learning has shown promise for this setting, but many successful contrastive methods rely on image augmentation techniques that do not apply to medical time series. This paper develops a training objective suited to the temporal structure of patient data.

Neighborhood contrastive learning supplements time-series augmentations by explicitly grouping contiguous time segments from the same patient. At the same time, it maintains information specific to the patient’s state. Both aspects matter to the proposed objective: neighboring observations should inform the learned representation, while distinctions in state should remain available for monitoring.

The experiments show a marked improvement over earlier applications of contrastive learning to medical time series. The finding supports tailoring the contrastive objective to the relationships present in the data, alongside choosing suitable augmentations. The paper’s contribution is a representation-learning approach that uses temporal proximity without discarding the state-specific information the monitoring task needs.
icml-2021-neighborhood-contrastive-learn.tldr: Neighborhood contrastive learning groups adjacent patient time segments while retaining state information, improving reported medical time-series representations.

paragraphs: Search-based path planning uses discrete decisions, which makes it difficult to train the entire planning process through a neural network. Neural A* addresses this obstacle by reformulating the A* search algorithm to be differentiable. It couples the search procedure with a convolutional encoder so that both can participate in end-to-end learning.

For each planning problem, the encoder produces a guidance map. The differentiable search then uses that map to find a path. Training encourages the search results to match expert-provided paths, allowing the learned guidance to respond to the outcomes of the search itself. The method retains an explicit search stage within the trainable planner.

Experiments show a better trade-off between search optimality and efficiency than state-of-the-art data-driven planners. The authors also demonstrate realistic human-trajectory prediction by running search-based planning directly on natural-image inputs. These results support combining learned guidance with differentiable search as a way to obtain accurate paths while controlling the amount of search required.
icml-2021-path-planning-using-neural-a-s.tldr: Neural A* learns guidance maps through differentiable search, improving the reported balance between path quality and search efficiency.

paragraphs: In multi-objective reinforcement learning, rewards form a vector representing several objectives. This paper studies competitive settings where success is measured by how close an agent’s average return vector comes to a target set. The learning problem therefore involves shaping several outcomes while responding to opponents and discovering the environment.

The authors develop statistically and computationally efficient algorithms that extend Blackwell’s approachability theorem to tabular reinforcement learning. Strategic exploration becomes an essential part of this extension. The algorithms are adaptive, and their guarantees remain valid even without Blackwell’s approachability condition. That qualification concerns the guarantees and does not imply every target set can always be reached.

When opponents follow fixed policies, the authors obtain an improved approach rate and additionally address minimizing a scalar cost at the same time. They relate this case to constrained reinforcement learning. The paper presents near-optimal theoretical guarantees and, to the authors’ knowledge, the first provably efficient algorithms for vector-valued Markov games.
icml-2021-provably-efficient-algorithms-.tldr: The paper develops efficient competitive reinforcement-learning algorithms with near-optimal guarantees for approaching target sets of vector-valued returns.

paragraphs: This paper considers online decisions with convex losses and constraints that may be violated temporarily but must hold over the long run. Its violation measure accumulates breaches without allowing comfortably feasible decisions to cancel them. This makes the guarantee track actual violations alongside regret, which measures performance relative to a comparison strategy.

The first algorithm offers a tunable trade-off. For c between zero and one, static regret is O(T^max{c,1−c}) and cumulative violation is O(T^((1−c)/2)), where T is the number of rounds. Under the additional assumption of strongly convex losses, both bounds become O(log T). The authors report improvements over existing theoretical results.

A second algorithm handles changing comparator sequences. It achieves optimal regret O(√(T(1+P_T))) and cumulative violation O(√T), where P_T measures the comparator’s total movement. This connects the performance guarantee to how much the reference decisions change over time. Numerical simulations illustrate the theoretical findings, supporting algorithms that manage both decision quality and accumulated constraint breaches.
icml-2021-regret-and-cumulative-constrai.tldr: New online convex optimization algorithms improve regret and cumulative violation bounds, with logarithmic bounds under strongly convex losses.

paragraphs: SinIR learns from a single natural image to support several image-manipulation tasks, including super-resolution, editing, harmonization, paint-to-image conversion, and style transfer. The framework uses a cascade of networks operating at multiple scales. Each network is trained to reconstruct the image at its own scale, making reconstruction the central learning objective.

The authors choose reconstruction because it reduces training complexity and running time compared with a generative adversarial objective. They also identify an accompanying output-quality problem. To address it, they introduce simple random pixel shuffling inspired by denoising autoencoders. This modification is also used to provide control over the resulting manipulation.

Quantitative evaluation shows competitive performance across multiple manipulation tasks. For 500-by-500 images, the authors report training 33.5 times faster than SinGAN, which addresses similar tasks. That speed comparison is tied to the stated image size. The findings show that a single-image reconstruction framework, combined with the proposed shuffling mechanism, can support varied manipulations with substantially faster reported training.
icml-2021-sinir-efficient-general-image-.tldr: SinIR combines multiscale single-image reconstruction with random pixel shuffling to support competitive image manipulation with much faster reported training.

paragraphs: The paper studies joint probability models for multivariate time series, with the aim of capturing relationships among entire series. Such models can also support questions about conditional independence: whether relationships remain after accounting for other information. The authors bring probabilistic circuits, previously explored extensively for tabular data, into this time-series setting.

Their Whittle sum-product networks use the Whittle approximation to express likelihood in the frequency domain. A complex-valued sum-product network then models the frequencies. This formulation allows conditional independence relationships among time series to be determined efficiently in the spectral domain. The frequency-based probability model is the central mechanism connecting the circuit approach to temporal data.

The authors also integrate these models into deep neural time-series systems, producing Whittle Networks. This makes likelihood available for training and for inspecting model behavior. Experiments show that the resulting networks can capture complex dependencies between series and provide a useful uncertainty measure, supporting both probabilistic analysis and neural-network applications.
icml-2021-whittle-networks-a-deep-likeli.tldr: Whittle Networks model time-series likelihoods in the frequency domain to capture dependencies and provide useful neural-network uncertainty estimates.
